The map's label for the kingdoms of north and central India ruled by warrior clans later called Rajputs ("sons of kings"), shown around 1000 to 1200. After the big empires of ancient India broke up, these lineages took power across what is now Rajasthan, Gujarat, Madhya Pradesh and the Ganges plain. The name Rajput for them became fixed only centuries later.

The main houses in these years:

  • the Chahamanas (Chauhans) of Ajmer and Delhi, whose last great king was Prithviraj Chauhan;
  • the Paramaras of Malwa, under the scholar king Bhoja;
  • the Chandelas, who built the Khajuraho temples;
  • the Chaulukyas of Gujarat and the Gahadavalas of Kannauj.

They fought each other often. From the west, Mahmud of Ghazni raided their temple cities and sacked Somnath in 1025. In 1192 Muhammad of Ghor beat Prithviraj at the second battle of Tarain, which opened the way for the Delhi Sultanate. Rajput states lived on in the hills and deserts of Rajputana for centuries after.
